rationale: A wins because it turns the same facts into more journalist-shaped beats, especially "Airbnb plugs into Concur and Ramp, putting the stay inside the expense report" instead of flattening that into product trivia. B has good bones, but "Airbnb calls business travel its fastest-growing segment. It won't say how big that segment actually is." crosses from skeptical into invented unless the update says Airbnb refused to disclose. That is the difference: A interrogates holes without making them facts; B sometimes writes the prosecution before it has evidence.
gaps_in_A: "rogue Airbnb bookings on personal cards" is plausible buyer pain, but the update does not state that behavior. Keep it as a reporting hypothesis, not a premise.
"Airbnb goes after managed corporate lodging spend with a tool it gives away" overstates "free for travelers"; the update does not prove it is free for employers or explain who pays.
"whether professional operators crowd out individual hosts" is a sharp question, but it is not grounded in the supplied facts. It belongs in proof-needed, not as implied conflict.
gaps_in_B: "It won't say how big that segment actually is" invents a refusal. The update only says the 71% growth is off a small base.
"higher-value guest segment" is not in the facts. Business travelers may be higher value, but no rate premium, spend level, or yield claim was supplied.
Refusing "A vendor-competition angle asking why Concur and Ramp" throws out a usable expense-stack story. The rivalry frame is weak, but the integration-plumbing beat is real.
"business-trends reporter or a features desk covering the future of corporate travel policy" is too soft. A features desk is not a sub-beat; it is where vague trend pitches go to nap.
